title: Supplemental Response of Petitioner Goldman Sachs Bank USA

No. 25-1408 
 
In the 
Supreme Court of the United States 
   
GOLDMAN SACHS BANK USA, d/b/a Marcus by 
Goldman Sachs,   
 Petitioner, 
V. 
RHEA ANN BROWN; GREGORY KEVIN MAZE,  
 Respondents. 
   
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI  
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT  
   
PETITIONER’S RESPONSE TO 
RESPONDENTS’ SUPPLEMENTAL BRIEF  
   
JEFF G. HAMMEL 
CHRISTOPHER HARRIS 
JASON HEGT  
LATHAM & WATKINS LLP 
1271 Avenue of the

Counsel for Petitioner

1 
 
 
Respondents’ supplemental brief is yet another 
effort to manufacture a vehicle problem where none 
exists.   
1.   Respondents argue (at 1) that the bankruptcy 
court’s September 10 dismissal of their complaint 
without prejudice makes this case unsuitable for 
review because further litigation will proceed on an 
amended complaint.  Not so. 
The bankruptcy court dismissed the complaint 
because—after more than two years of litigation—
respondents still had not adequately pleaded actual 
damages.  Op. 7-27, Brown v. Goldman Sachs Bank 
USA, Adv. Proc. No. 24-7009 (B ankr. W.D. Va. Sept. 
10, 2026),  ECF No. 62.  GS Bank welcomes that 
ruling, which confirms the weakness of respondents’ 
claims.  But the ruling does nothing to resolve the 
forum dispute presented here.  Respondents make 
clear (at 1-2) that they will amend and continue 
pressing the same Section 362(k) claims the Fourth 
Circuit held need not be arbitrated.  If and when they 
lose (again) in bankruptcy court, they will presumably 
appeal to the district court and, if necessary, to the 
court of appeals.  The Fourth Circuit’s flawed 
arbitration ruling thus threatens still more rounds of 
briefing and decisions, potentially spanning months 
or years. 
Avoiding that prolonged judicial process is one of 
the key reasons parties adopt arbitration agreements 
in the first place—and why enforcing such 
agreements is so important.  The FAA accordingly 
directs courts to move arbitrable disputes “out of court 
and into arbitration as quickly and easily as possible.”  
Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 
460 U.S. 1, 22 (1983).  The prospect of still more 
litigation thus strengthens, rather than weakens, the

2 
 
 
case for review.  If respondents’ claims proceed, they 
should proceed in arbitration as the parties agreed. 
2.   Respondents devote much of their 
supplemental brief (at 1-2) to rearguing whether the 
original complaint asserted an independent claim 
under Section 105(a).  It didn’t—but this issue is a 
sideshow that doesn’t bear on certiorari in any event.   
As GS Bank explained, respondents never brought 
a freestanding contempt proceeding under Section 
105(a).  Reply.Br.10.  Instead, they brought a putative 
nationwide class action asserting a single cause of 
action under Section 362(k).  CA4 Appendix (JA) 27 
(¶ 71). 
Respondents rely (at 2) on two snippets from the 
complaint: one paragraph citing Section 105 among 
several sources of remedial authority, and a lone 
reference to “contempt” in the prayer for relief.  
Neither establishes an independent Section 105 
claim.  The Section 105 reference appears within the 
complaint’s sole cause of action under Section 362 .  
JA27 (¶ 71).  And the word  “contempt” appears only 
in the prayer for relief alongside an array of requested 
remedies.  JA30.  No count alleges contempt or pleads 
any distinct Section 105 theory.   
More fundamentally, contempt was unavailable in 
this putative class adversary proceeding to begin 
with.  As GS Bank explained, contempt under Section 
105 must be sought by motion in the underlying 
bankruptcy case.  Reply.Br.9; see, e.g. , Green Point 
Credit, LLC v. McLean (In re McLean), 794 F.3d 1313, 
1326 (11th Cir. 2015); Shockley v. Moellmer (In re 
Davis), 2026 WL 927645, at *3 (Bankr. S.D. Ohio Mar. 
30, 2026).  Respondents now dispute that rule, but 
ignore their own conce ssions below:  Under the

3 
 
 
majority rule, Section 105(a)  contempt is “limited to 
the cases before the court where the matter is raised” 
and cannot supply the nationwide class relief (or 
punitive damages) they seek here.  MTD Hr’g 10, 13, 
Adv. Proc. No. 24-7009 (Aug. 13, 2026)1; see also, e.g., 
Appellees.Br.58, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. 
Brown, No. 24-cv-490 (W.D. Va. Nov. 22, 2024),  Dkt. 
No. 23 (noting circuit court “trends” holding that 
bankruptcy court would “lack authority to impose 
sanctions under § 105(a) fo r conduct outside of the 
Court’s jurisdiction,” citing PHH Mortg. Corp. v. 
Sensenich (In re Gravel) , 6 F.4th 503 (2d Cir. 2021), 
cert. denied, 142 S. Ct. 2829 (2022); Crocker v. Navient 
Sols., LLC (In re Crocker), 941 F.3d 206, 208 (5th Cir. 
2019)); see also MTD Hr’g 10 (noting that Congress 
created the Section 362(k) private right of action 
because “contempt remedies were overly limited”).   
Those limitations on cont empt are precisely why 
respondents pursued nationwide class relief through 
Section 362(k)’s  private cause of action, instead of 
through a contempt motion.  They’re also why 
respondents are wrong to pretend that Section 362(k) 
and contempt are somehow interchangeable 
substitutes.  Reply.Br.11. 
Ultimately, Section 105(a) is a red herring that 
should not obscure the need for review on the Section 
362(k) issue.  The questi on presented is whether 
respondents’ Section 362(k) claims must be 
arbitrated.  Even if respondents amend to add a 
standalone contempt theory under Section 105—and 
then somehow overcome the procedural and 
 
1   GS Bank possesses a certifie d reporters’ transcript of the 
motion-to-dismiss hearing and can provide it to the Court at its 
request.

4 
 
 
substantive obstacles to sustaining it—their Section 
362(k) claims would remain in court under the Fourth 
Circuit’s flawed no-arbitration rule.  The judgment 
below therefore continues to bar GS Bank from 
enforcing its arbitration agreements as to those 
claims, and the conflict with MBNA America Bank, 
N.A. v. Hill , 436 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2006), remains 
unresolved. 
CONCLUSION 
The petition should be granted.
